title: The Prairie State
bigQuestion: How did the land of Illinois get the way it is, and how do people use it?

story.title: Grass Taller Than You
story.kicker: Step into a restored prairie in June. The grass closes over your head, and the sky goes away.
paragraphs: It is a hot morning in June. A fourth-grade class steps off a bus at a nature preserve an hour from Chicago. A ranger leads them down a mowed path. On both sides, grass rises higher and higher. By the middle of the path, the tallest kids cannot see over it. The grass is called big bluestem. By August it will stand eight feet tall.

The ranger stops. She tells the class to be quiet and listen. Bees hum. A red-winged blackbird calls from a stalk. The wind moves through the grass and makes a sound like the ocean. Purple flowers called coneflowers poke up between the blades. Nobody planted them. They grew here on their own.

Then the ranger says something surprising. Two hundred years ago, most of Illinois looked like this. Not corn. Not soybeans. Not streets and houses. Grass and flowers, from horizon to horizon, taller than a person on a horse. Travelers wrote that they felt like they were sailing on a green sea.

Today almost all of that prairie is gone. Farmers plowed it up because the soil under it was some of the richest on Earth. That soil still feeds the state and much of the world. This small patch was saved and replanted so people could see what the land used to be. The ranger asks the class to look down at the dirt. It is nearly black.

That black dirt is the reason Illinois is called the Prairie State. It is the reason for the farms, the towns, the railroads, and in a way, the city of Chicago. To understand Illinois, you have to start with the land.
story.think: If you could see Illinois from an airplane two hundred years ago and today, what would look different? What might look the same?

lessons.title: Neighbors and Borders
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois sits in the middle of the country, with five neighbor states and a Great Lake around it.
reading: Find Illinois on a map of the United States. It is near the center of the country, in the region called the Midwest. It is shaped a little like a long arrowhead pointing south. From the top of the state to the bottom is about 380 miles. That is a long drive, more than six hours on the highway.

Illinois has five *neighbor* states. Wisconsin is to the north. Iowa and Missouri are to the west. Kentucky is to the south. Indiana is to the east. A line where one state ends and another begins is called a *border*. Some of these borders are straight lines drawn on paper. Others follow rivers.

In the northeast corner, Illinois touches Lake Michigan. Across the lake is the state of Michigan. Chicago, the biggest city in Illinois, sits on the lake shore. The capital, where the state government works, is Springfield, near the middle of the state.

words.d: a state, town or person right next to you
the line where one state or country ends and another begins
the city where a state's or country's government works

look.title: The Shape of the State
look.text: Look at a map of Illinois. Trace the east side with your finger. The top part is a straight line. Then, partway down, the line starts to wiggle. Now trace the whole west side. It wiggles the entire way. The wiggles are rivers.
look.prompt: Why might some borders be straight and others wiggle?

check.q: Which state is directly north of Illinois?
check.why: Wisconsin is to the north. Kentucky is south, Iowa is west and Indiana is east.

check.q: What is the capital of Illinois?
check.why: Springfield, near the middle of the state, is where the state government works. Chicago is the biggest city but not the capital.

check.q: What is a border?
choices: The line where one state ends and another begins
The biggest city in a state
check.why: A border is the dividing line between two states or countries. Some are straight, some follow rivers.

check.q: About how far is it from the top of Illinois to the bottom?
check.why: The state is about 380 miles long from north to south, more than six hours of driving.

lessons.title: Rivers That Draw the Lines
lessons.mainIdea: Great rivers form most of the borders of Illinois and carry its goods to the sea.
reading: The wiggly borders of Illinois are rivers. The *Mississippi River* runs down the whole west side of the state. It separates Illinois from Iowa and Missouri. It is one of the longest rivers in the world. Farmers have shipped corn down the Mississippi on boats for two hundred years. At the very bottom of the state, at the town of Cairo, the Ohio River joins it.

The *Ohio River* forms the southern border with Kentucky. The Wabash River forms the lower part of the eastern border with Indiana. Before there were roads or trains, rivers were the highways. A flatboat could float a family and everything they owned downstream.

One big river runs through the middle of the state instead of around it. The *Illinois River* starts near Chicago and flows southwest across the state to the Mississippi. Long ago, Native people, French traders and settlers all used it as a path. Today barges still carry grain, coal and steel on it.

words.d: the huge river that forms the western border of Illinois
the river that forms the southern border of Illinois
the river that flows across the middle of the state to the Mississippi
a long, flat boat that carries heavy loads like grain or coal

look.title: Rivers of Illinois, Roughly
look.cite: U.S. Geological Survey, standard rounded lengths
look.prompt: Which river is the longest? Which of these four rivers stays mostly inside Illinois?

check.q: Which river forms the western border of Illinois?
check.why: The Mississippi runs down the whole west side of the state, between Illinois and Iowa and Missouri.

check.q: Where does the Ohio River join the Mississippi?
choices: At Cairo, at the bottom of the state
check.why: The two great rivers meet at the southern tip of Illinois, at the town of Cairo.

check.q: Why were rivers so important before roads and trains?
choices: They were the highways for moving people and goods
They had no fish in them
check.why: A boat could float a family or a load of corn downstream long before there were roads.

check.q: Which river flows through the middle of the state instead of around it?
check.why: The Illinois River starts near Chicago and crosses the state to the Mississippi. The other three are border rivers.

lessons.title: Lake Michigan
lessons.mainIdea: Lake Michigan gives Chicago its drinking water, its harbor and its cool breezes.
reading: Stand on the shore in Chicago and look east. You cannot see the other side. Lake Michigan is so big that it looks like an ocean, but the water is fresh, not salty. It is one of the five *Great Lakes*, which together hold about one fifth of all the fresh surface water on Earth. Illinois touches only Lake Michigan, along a short strip of shore in the northeast corner.

The lake is why Chicago is where it is. Ships carried goods from the East across the lakes. They unloaded them at Chicago. From there, the goods went by canal or train to the rest of the country. The lake is also where Chicago gets its drinking water. Big water plants clean it and pipe it to millions of homes.

The lake changes the weather too. In summer, a breeze off the cold water cools the lakefront. In winter, air blowing across the lake picks up moisture and drops heavy *lake-effect snow* on towns downwind. Illinois built parks and beaches along much of the shore so everyone can reach the water.

words.d: five huge freshwater lakes between the United States and Canada
water that is not salty, the kind people can drink
heavy snow made when cold air picks up moisture from a lake

look.title: A Cold Morning by the Lake
look.text: It is a June morning in Chicago. At a school ten miles from the lake, kids are in shorts and it is 80 degrees. At a school one block from the lake, kids are wearing sweatshirts and it is 65 degrees. A cool wind is blowing in from the water.
look.prompt: Why is it so much cooler near the lake? What do you think happens on a cold winter day?

check.q: How is Lake Michigan different from an ocean?
choices: Its water is fresh, not salty
check.why: Lake Michigan looks like an ocean, but its water is fresh. That is why Chicago can drink it.

check.q: Where does Chicago get its drinking water?
check.why: Water plants clean lake water and pipe it to millions of homes.

check.q: Why did the lake help Chicago grow?
choices: The lake was good for swimming
The lake made the land flat
Ships could unload goods there and send them on by canal or train
check.why: Chicago became a meeting point for ships from the East and trains and canals heading west.

check.q: What causes lake-effect snow?
choices: Cold air picking up moisture as it crosses the lake
Snow falling from the lake bottom
check.why: Cold winter air blows across the lake, picks up moisture and drops it as snow on towns downwind.

lessons.title: Ice Flattens the Land
lessons.mainIdea: Giant sheets of ice called glaciers scraped most of Illinois flat and left behind rich, crushed rock.
reading: Why is Illinois so flat? The answer is ice. Long ago, during the *Ice Age*, the Earth was colder than it is now. Snow piled up in Canada year after year and never melted. It squeezed into ice sheets more than a mile thick. Those ice sheets, called *glaciers*, slowly crept south like frozen bulldozers.

The glaciers pushed into Illinois more than once. The last big ice sheet melted away from northern Illinois roughly fifteen thousand years ago. As the ice moved, it scraped off hills. It filled in valleys. It ground rocks into fine dust. When it melted, it left that ground-up rock spread across the land. How do we know? The rocks and gravel under Illinois soil match rocks from Canada.

Not every part of the state was covered. The ice never reached the far south. So the Shawnee Hills there are still rough and rocky. A small corner in the northwest was also missed. It has steep hills too. Everywhere else, the glaciers left flat land. They also left a deep layer of crushed rock. That layer would become some of the best soil in the world.

words.d: a long time when Earth was colder and ice covered much of the land
a huge, thick sheet of ice that moves slowly over the land

look.title: High and Low Points of Illinois
look.prompt: The highest and lowest points are less than 1,000 feet apart. What does that tell you about the shape of the state?

check.q: What flattened most of Illinois?
choices: Glaciers, huge sheets of moving ice
check.why: During the Ice Age, thick ice sheets scraped the land flat and ground up the rocks.

check.q: How do we know glaciers came from the north?
choices: Rocks under Illinois soil match rocks from Canada
check.why: The crushed rock the ice left behind matches rock from far to the north, where the ice started.

check.q: Why are the Shawnee Hills in the south still rough and rocky?
choices: The glaciers never reached that far south
The glaciers pushed the hills up
check.why: The ice stopped before the far south. The hills there were never scraped flat.

check.q: What did the glaciers leave behind when they melted?
choices: A layer of ground-up rock that became rich soil
check.why: The melting ice dropped crushed rock across the land. Over time it turned into deep, rich soil.

lessons.title: Grass, Roots and Black Soil
lessons.mainIdea: Thousands of years of prairie grass built the deep black soil that makes Illinois farmland so rich.
reading: After the ice melted, grass grew on the crushed rock. Not short lawn grass. Tallgrass *prairie*: big bluestem, Indian grass and switchgrass, along with hundreds of kinds of wildflowers. The roots went deep, sometimes ten feet or more. Every year the grass died back and rotted. Every year the roots grew again. Fires set by lightning, and by Native people, burned off the dead stalks and kept trees from taking over.

This went on for thousands of years. All that rotting grass and root built up a thick layer of dark, crumbly earth called *topsoil*. In some places the black topsoil in Illinois is more than three feet deep. Rich soil is why the state's nickname is the Prairie State. It is also why Illinois grows so much food.

Settlers arrived in the early 1800s. Prairie then covered about two thirds of Illinois. Their iron plows stuck in the tough roots. Then, in 1837, a blacksmith named John Deere made a smooth steel plow. He worked in Grand Detour, Illinois. His plow cut clean through the sod. Within a few decades, nearly all the prairie was plowed into farms. Today less than one percent of the original prairie is left, in small preserves.

words.d: a wide, open land of tall grasses and wildflowers with few trees
the dark top layer of earth where plants grow best
the top layer of soil held together by grass roots

look.title: A Visitor Sees the Prairie, 1842
look.text: The English writer Charles Dickens visited a prairie in Illinois in 1842. He wrote that the grass stretched to the edge of the sky in every direction, with the sun setting on it like the sun over the sea, and that it was lonely and wild and huge. He admitted that he had expected to feel more amazed than he did.
look.prompt: Dickens compared the prairie to the sea. What do a prairie and an ocean have in common?

check.q: What built the deep black topsoil of Illinois?
choices: Thousands of years of prairie grass and roots rotting
check.why: Prairie plants died back and regrew every year for thousands of years. The rotted plants became rich topsoil.

check.q: Why did fires help the prairie?
choices: They killed all the grass forever
They burned dead stalks and kept trees from taking over
check.why: Fires cleared the dead grass and stopped forests from growing. The deep roots survived and the prairie grew back.

check.q: Why did John Deere's steel plow matter?
choices: It was the first plow ever made
It could plant corn by itself
It cut through tough prairie roots that stuck iron plows
check.why: The smooth steel plow cut clean through the thick sod, so settlers could turn prairie into farms.

check.q: How much of the original Illinois prairie is left today?
check.why: Nearly all the prairie was plowed into farms. Only small preserves remain.

lessons.title: Chicago and the North
lessons.mainIdea: Northern Illinois holds Chicago and most of the state's people, jobs and factories.
reading: Geographers divide Illinois into *regions*, areas that share a way of life or a kind of land. The northern region is where most people live. About two out of every three Illinoisans live in Chicago and its suburbs, which spread across several counties. Chicago itself has about 2.7 million people, more than any other city in the Midwest.

Trains, highways and two big airports meet in Chicago. Factories, banks, hospitals and offices give people jobs. Rockford, in the north, makes machine parts and tools. Farther west, the Rock River winds through hilly country. The northwest corner, near Galena, has the highest ground in the state.

Northern Illinois is not all city. Just outside the *suburbs*, the land turns quickly to corn and soybean fields. Many towns are a mix: a train station to the city on one side, a grain elevator on the other.

words.d: an area of land whose parts share something, like a kind of land or way of life
a town just outside a big city where many people live and travel into the city

look.title: Biggest Cities in Illinois, About 2020
look.prompt: How many times bigger is Chicago than the next biggest city? Which cities on this list are suburbs of Chicago?

check.q: What is a region?
choices: An area whose parts share something, like the land or way of life
check.why: Geographers group land into regions that share features, such as flat farmland or a big city area.

check.q: About how many Illinoisans live in Chicago and its suburbs?
check.why: Roughly two thirds of the state's people live in the Chicago area.

check.q: Which of these is a job center in the north?
check.why: Rockford, in northern Illinois, is known for making machine parts and tools.

check.q: What would you likely see just outside the Chicago suburbs?
check.why: The land turns quickly from suburbs to farmland. Many towns have both a train station and a grain elevator.

lessons.title: Farmland and the Shawnee Hills
lessons.mainIdea: Central Illinois is flat farmland, while the far south rises into rocky, forested hills.
reading: Drive south from Chicago and the land opens up. Central Illinois is the flattest, richest farmland in the state. Fields of corn and soybeans run to the horizon. Farmhouses, grain silos and small towns break them up. Springfield, the capital, sits here. So does Peoria, on the Illinois River. So do Champaign and Urbana, home of the state's biggest university.

Keep driving south and the land changes. The glaciers never reached the bottom of the state, so the ground begins to roll and then rise. The *Shawnee Hills* cross southern Illinois from river to river. They are covered by the Shawnee National Forest, with sandstone cliffs, canyons and waterfalls. Some people call this region Little Egypt, and the town at the very tip is named Cairo.

Southern Illinois has a milder, wetter climate. Peach and apple orchards grow well. Coal lies under much of the region. Because the south and the north are so different, people from the two ends of the state sometimes feel like they live in different places. In a way, they do.

words.d: the rocky, forested hills across the far southern part of Illinois
a tall round tower where farmers store grain
a field of fruit trees

look.title: Two Postcards
look.text: Postcard one shows a field so flat that a grain elevator ten miles away looks close. The sky takes up most of the picture. Postcard two shows a hiker on a sandstone cliff above a green forest, with a creek far below. Both were mailed from Illinois.
look.prompt: Which region is each postcard from? What clue tells you?

check.q: What is central Illinois mostly used for?
check.why: Central Illinois has the flattest, richest farmland in the state.

check.q: Why is the far south of Illinois hilly?
choices: The glaciers did not reach that far, so nothing flattened it
The rivers pushed the land up
check.why: The ice sheets stopped before the southern tip. The old hills there were never scraped down.

check.q: What covers much of the Shawnee Hills?
choices: The Shawnee National Forest, with cliffs and canyons
check.why: The national forest spreads across the hills, with sandstone cliffs, canyons and waterfalls.

check.q: Which crop grows well in the milder south?
check.why: Southern Illinois has a milder, wetter climate, which suits fruit orchards.

lessons.title: Seasons, Storms and Floods
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois has hot summers, cold winters and dangerous tornadoes and floods.
reading: Illinois is far from any ocean, so nothing keeps its weather steady. Summers are hot and sticky. Winters are cold, with snow that can shut down roads. Spring and fall bring quick changes. This pattern is called a *continental climate*. The south is a little warmer and wetter than the north, which is why peaches grow there and not near Chicago.

Spring in Illinois brings *tornadoes*. Warm, wet air from the Gulf of Mexico crashes into cold, dry air from the north. The two twist together. A spinning funnel of wind can drop from a storm cloud. The worst tornado in United States history struck in 1925. It tore across Missouri, Illinois and Indiana in one afternoon. It killed about seven hundred people. Most of them were in southern Illinois towns like Murphysboro.

Rivers bring *floods*. In the wet summer of 1993, the Mississippi and Illinois rivers rose over their banks for weeks. Water covered farms and towns. Today, towns build tall earthen walls called levees along rivers. Schools practice tornado drills. Knowing the weather is part of living in Illinois.

words.d: weather far from an ocean, with hot summers and cold winters
a spinning funnel of wind that drops from a storm cloud
when a river rises over its banks and covers the land
a wall of earth built along a river to hold back floods

look.title: The Sky Turns Green
look.text: It is a warm April afternoon in a small town in central Illinois. The air feels heavy and still. The sky to the west turns a strange greenish gray. Then the town's siren begins to wail. In the school, the teacher says one word, and every student walks quickly to the inside hallway and crouches by the wall.
look.prompt: What is happening? Why is an inside hallway with no windows the safest place?

check.q: Why does Illinois have hot summers and cold winters?
choices: It is very close to an ocean
It is far from any ocean, so nothing steadies the weather
It is near the South Pole
check.why: Land far from the sea heats up and cools down fast. This is called a continental climate.

check.q: What makes tornadoes form in spring?
choices: Warm wet air from the south crashing into cold dry air from the north
check.why: When warm, moist air and cold, dry air meet and twist, a funnel can drop from the storm cloud.

check.q: What happened in the summer of 1993?
choices: The Mississippi and Illinois rivers flooded for weeks
check.why: Weeks of rain sent the rivers over their banks, covering farms and towns.

check.q: What is a levee for?
check.why: A levee is a wall of earth along a river that keeps high water off the land.

lessons.title: Soil, Coal and Water
lessons.mainIdea: The most valuable natural resources in Illinois are its soil, its coal and its water.
reading: A *natural resource* is something from nature that people use. The most valuable one in Illinois is not gold or oil. It is dirt. The deep black topsoil left by the prairie makes Illinois one of the best places on Earth to grow food. Farmland covers about three fourths of the state.

Under the soil lies *coal*. Coal is a black rock. It formed from swamp plants that were buried and squeezed for millions of years. It burns hot. People used it to heat homes and to make electricity. Illinois has some of the largest coal deposits in the country. Most of it lies under the central and southern parts of the state. Coal mining gave many towns their jobs. But burning coal dirties the air. So less coal is mined today than in the past.

Water is the third great resource. Lake Michigan gives drinking water to Chicago and its suburbs. Rivers carry barges and water the fields. Under the ground, layers of sand and gravel left by the glaciers hold water. Towns pump it up through wells. Rich soil, coal and water: the glaciers and the prairie gave Illinois all three.

words.d: something from nature that people use, like soil, water or coal
a black rock that burns, made from plants buried long ago
a deep hole dug to reach water underground

look.title: Three Jobs, One State
look.text: Maria's grandfather worked in a coal mine near Carbondale in the south. Her mother runs a farm near Bloomington in the center of the state. Maria's aunt works at the water plant in Chicago that cleans lake water for the city.
look.prompt: Which natural resource does each person's job depend on? Which resource will still be there in a thousand years, and which could run out?

check.q: What is the most valuable natural resource in Illinois?
check.why: The deep black topsoil makes Illinois one of the best food-growing places on Earth.

check.q: Where did coal come from?
choices: Swamp plants buried and squeezed for millions of years
check.why: Coal formed from ancient plants that were buried under the ground and pressed for a very long time.

check.q: Why is less coal mined in Illinois today than in the past?
choices: It is too hard to reach
check.why: Illinois still has large coal deposits, but burning coal pollutes, so people use less of it.

check.q: How do many Illinois towns far from the lake get water?
choices: They ship it from the ocean
They pump it from underground through wells
check.why: Sand and gravel left by glaciers hold water underground. Towns reach it with wells.

lessons.title: Corn and Soybeans
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois farms grow corn and soybeans that feed animals and people around the world.
reading: Look out the window on a drive across Illinois in August. Row after row of tall green *corn*. Then a lower, bushier field of *soybeans*. Then corn again. These two crops cover most of the farmland in the state. Illinois is usually one of the top two states in the country for both, along with Iowa.

Very little of that corn is the sweet corn you eat off the cob. Most is field corn. It feeds cows, pigs and chickens. It is ground into cornmeal and corn syrup. Some is turned into a fuel called ethanol and mixed into gasoline. Soybeans are crushed for oil and for protein-rich animal feed. Both crops are shipped by train and barge, down the Mississippi to the port at New Orleans, and on to countries around the world.

Farming has changed. In 1900, most families in Illinois lived on farms and worked with horses. Today one farmer with a giant machine can plant or *harvest* hundreds of acres in a day. Fewer than one in fifty Illinoisans farms now. But the state still grows food for millions of people who have never seen a cornfield.

words.d: a tall grain plant; most Illinois corn feeds animals or becomes fuel or syrup
a bushy bean plant grown for oil and animal feed
to gather a crop when it is ripe

look.title: What Illinois Farmland Grows
look.unit: acres in a typical recent year, rounded
look.prompt: Corn and soybeans together cover about twenty million acres. About how many acres of wheat would fit in that space?

check.q: What are the two main crops of Illinois?
check.why: Corn and soybeans cover most of the farmland in the state.

check.q: What happens to most Illinois corn?
choices: It is eaten fresh off the cob
It feeds animals or becomes syrup or fuel
It is used to build houses
check.why: Most is field corn, which feeds cows, pigs and chickens or is made into corn syrup and ethanol.

check.q: How does Illinois grain reach other countries?
choices: It does not leave the state
By train and barge down the Mississippi to New Orleans, then by ship
check.why: Barges carry grain down the river to the port at New Orleans, where ships take it overseas.

check.q: How has farming changed since 1900?
choices: Far fewer people farm, and big machines do the work
More people farm now than before
check.why: In 1900 most families farmed with horses. Today fewer than one in fifty Illinoisans farms, using big machines.

lessons.title: People Change the Land
lessons.mainIdea: People have reshaped Illinois by draining, plowing, building and even turning a river around.
reading: The land shapes people, but people also shape the land. Much of the Illinois prairie was wet and swampy in spring. Farmers dug ditches and buried clay pipes called *drain tiles* to carry the water away. Thousands of miles of them still run under the fields. Without them, much of central Illinois could not be farmed.

Chicago made the biggest change of all. The Chicago River used to flow into Lake Michigan. It carried the city's waste into its own drinking water. People got sick. So engineers dug a deep canal. In 1900 they made the river flow backward, away from the lake and toward the Mississippi. Chicago also filled in part of the lake to build parks. It even raised whole streets out of the mud.

Every change has a cost. Draining the wetlands took away homes for ducks and fish. Plowing the prairie erased it. Coal mines left scars. Today people work to *restore* some of what was lost, replanting prairie and cleaning rivers. The question for your generation is how to use the land and still take care of it.

words.d: a buried pipe that carries water away from wet farmland
a waterway dug by people for boats or for moving water
to bring something back to the way it was

look.title: A Settler Describes the Wet Prairie
look.text: A writer who lived in Illinois in the 1830s described the spring prairie as a place where the ground shook under a horse's feet and water stood in every low spot, so that travelers rode for miles with the horses' legs in water and the air full of biting flies.
look.cite: Eliza Farnham, Life in Prairie Land, 1846, paraphrased
look.prompt: What problem did farmers have to solve before they could plant this land? How did they solve it?

check.q: Why did farmers bury drain tiles under their fields?
choices: To carry water away from wet, swampy land
To bring water to dry land
check.why: Much of the prairie was wet in spring. Drain tiles carried the water off so the land could be farmed.

check.q: What did Chicago do to its river in 1900?
choices: Made it flow backward, away from the lake
Made it flow into Lake Michigan
check.why: Engineers dug a canal so the river carried waste away from the lake and toward the Mississippi.

check.q: Why did Chicago reverse its river?
choices: The river was carrying waste into the city's drinking water
check.why: The river dumped waste into the lake, where the city got its water, and people got sick.

check.q: What is one cost of draining the wetlands?
choices: Ducks and fish lost their homes
check.why: Every change has a cost. Wet places that animals needed were turned into fields.

review.q: Which of these is NOT a neighbor of Illinois?
review.why: Illinois borders Wisconsin, Iowa, Missouri, Kentucky and Indiana. Ohio is farther east.

review.q: Which river forms the southern border of Illinois?
review.why: The Ohio River separates Illinois from Kentucky and joins the Mississippi at Cairo.

review.q: Why is most of Illinois flat?
choices: Glaciers scraped it flat during the Ice Age
It was once the bottom of Lake Michigan
review.why: Ice sheets more than a mile thick ground down hills and filled valleys.

review.q: What made the topsoil of Illinois so rich?
choices: Thousands of years of prairie grass rotting into the ground
review.why: Prairie plants and their deep roots died and regrew for thousands of years, building deep black soil.

review.q: Where do about two thirds of Illinoisans live?
review.why: The Chicago area, in the northern region, holds most of the state's people.

review.q: What kind of weather danger comes when warm Gulf air meets cold northern air?
review.why: The clash of warm, wet air and cold, dry air can twist into a tornado.

review.q: Which three natural resources does the chapter call the most valuable in Illinois?
review.why: Rich soil, large coal deposits and plentiful water are the state's key resources.

review.q: What is one way people changed the land of Illinois?
choices: They built mountains in the south
They made the Chicago River flow backward
review.why: In 1900 engineers reversed the Chicago River so waste flowed away from the city's drinking water.
